# How to Spot an AI Scam Call, Fake Email, or Deepfake Voice Today

> **In short:** AI can copy a voice from a short audio clip, and scammers can make any name or number show up on your caller ID, so a familiar voice or number proves nothing. Hang up, call back on a number you look up yourself, and never pay with gift cards, crypto, wire transfers, or payment apps.

By the end of this guide you'll know the warning signs of a scam phone call, how to check a caller safely, and what to do if you already paid or shared something. Fake emails and cloned voices follow the same pattern as scam calls, so the same habits cover them. Nothing here requires buying or installing anything.

## Before you start
- A phone (mobile or landline) and an email account you check regularly.
- About 10 minutes in total, mostly to set up one protection you can use for years.
- One or two trusted people, such as a family member or a close friend, for the family safe-word step.

## Step 1 — Learn the four warning signs of a scam call
Whoever is calling, listen for the four signs the FTC lists for scams: the caller **pretends to be someone you trust** (a government agency, a company, a charity, or a relative); they describe **a problem or a prize** (you owe money, your account has a problem, a family member is in trouble, you've won something but must pay a fee); they **pressure you to act right now**, sometimes by telling you not to hang up; and they **demand a specific way to pay**. One sign is enough reason to end the call. Honest businesses give you time to decide, and real government agencies don't call out of the blue to threaten you or to ask for your Social Security number.
💬 Example: "This is the fraud department. Your account is in danger, so stay on the line and buy gift cards to protect your money" → that is three signs in one sentence → hang up.
You'll know it worked when you can name which of the four signs a suspicious call showed.

## Step 2 — Don't trust the caller ID or the voice
Scammers can make any name or number appear on your caller ID, so a call that looks local, or that shows your bank's name, could come from anywhere in the world. A voice is no safer: the FTC warns that scammers can clone a loved one's voice (an AI that copies how someone sounds) from a short audio clip. So when a call is unexpected, treat the name on the screen and the sound of the voice as claims to check, not as proof. The same goes for emails and texts, which can now be written in perfect grammar: judge a message by what it asks you to do, not by how polished it looks.
💬 Example: Your screen shows the name of your bank and a calm, professional voice says your account is at risk → that proves nothing yet → go to Step 3.
You'll know it worked when you wait to verify the caller before you answer any question or follow any instruction.

## Step 3 — Hang up and call back on a number you look up yourself
If someone calls about your account, your bank, a delivery, or a government payment, end the call and contact the organization yourself. Use the number on your card, on your statement, or on the organization's official website — never a number the caller gave you or one shown on caller ID. A real organization can handle a call back. The same rule works for emails and texts: don't click links in an unexpected message, even if it seems to come from a company you use, and go to the company's website or app on your own instead. Treat a request to read out a one-time code, a password, or a card number like any other request for personal or financial information: don't share it with someone who contacted you.
💬 Example: "Hello, this is your bank's fraud department" → hang up → dial the number on the back of your card.
You'll know it worked when you reached the organization on a number you found yourself and the person there can tell you whether the first call was real.

## Step 4 — Check a "family emergency" call without trusting the voice
If a call claims to come from a relative in trouble, don't trust the voice alone. Hang up, or say you'll call back, and call that relative on a number you already know is correct. If you can't reach them, check with another family member or one of their friends, even if the caller asked you to keep it secret. If you can't hang up, ask a question only the real person would know. A request for money by wire, cryptocurrency, or gift card is a major red flag, whoever seems to be asking.
💬 Example: "Grandma, it's me, I was in an accident, please send money" → hang up → call your grandchild's saved number → if there's no answer, call their parent.
You'll know it worked when you have heard from the real person, or from another relative, before any money moves.

## Step 5 — Never pay the way scammers ask, and slow down
Scammers prefer payments that are hard to reverse. Anyone who insists on **gift cards, cryptocurrency (including through a crypto ATM), wire transfers or other money transfer services, or a payment app** is a scammer, and you should never deposit a check and send money back either. Don't act under pressure: legitimate businesses give you time to decide. Before you do anything else, describe the situation to a friend, a family member, or a neighbor, because saying it out loud often shows what's wrong.
💬 Example: "Pay this fee now or your account closes in five minutes" → don't pay → call someone you trust and tell them about it.
You'll know it worked when you have told someone you trust about the call before you do anything else.

## Step 6 — Set up a family safe word today
The FBI recommends creating a secret word or phrase with your family to verify identity. Pick one unusual word with one or two people you trust, and agree that any "emergency" call must include it before any money moves. A short group chat, a text, or an in-person conversation is enough — no app or password manager needed. A scammer using a cloned voice won't know your word, and your real relative will. If your family is spread out, agree on a private question with a private answer instead. Write the word down once, share it only with the people who need it, and don't post it anywhere online. The FBI also suggests limiting how much of your voice and image you post publicly and keeping your social media accounts private.
💬 Example: Text your sister: "If anyone calls saying they're me and needs money, ask them for our safe word. The word is platypus."
You'll know it worked when at least two people in your circle can say the word without looking it up.

## Step 7 — Know what to do if you already paid or shared something
Hang up, stop replying, and act quickly — there is nothing to be embarrassed about. If you paid, contact the company or bank behind the payment right away and ask for your money back: the card issuer for a credit or debit card, the gift card company for a gift card, the transfer provider or your bank for a wire transfer, the app for a payment app, and the exchange or ATM operator for cryptocurrency (recovery is harder there). If you shared a password, create a new strong one, change it anywhere else you used it, and turn on two-factor authentication. If you gave out your Social Security number, go to IdentityTheft.gov. Be wary of anyone who offers to recover your lost money for a fee, because that is likely a second scam.
Then **report it**, even if you lost nothing: report scams at reportfraud.ftc.gov, use donotcall.gov to report an unwanted call, forward phishing emails to reportphishing@apwg.org and phishing texts to 7726, and file a report with the FBI's Internet Crime Complaint Center at ic3.gov. Outside the US, contact your local police or consumer protection agency.
💬 Example: Realized mid-call that the "bank agent" was fake → hung up → called the number on my card → told them what happened → filed a report at reportfraud.ftc.gov.
You'll know it worked when the company behind the payment knows what happened, you have filed one report, and any password you shared has been changed.

## Common mistakes
- **Trusting caller ID or a familiar voice.** Scammers can fake the name and number, and AI can fake the voice. Hang up and call back on a number you looked up yourself.
- **Staying on the line because the caller says you must.** Pressure to keep talking or to decide right now is a warning sign. Pausing is always safe.
- **Calling back the number the caller or the message gave you.** It leads to the scammer. Use the number on your card, your statement, or the official website.
- **Paying with a gift card, crypto, a wire transfer, or a payment app "just this once."** Real businesses and agencies don't demand these.
- **Skipping the family safe word because "it won't happen to us."** Setting it up takes a minute. Treat it like a smoke detector: boring to install, useful when it matters.

## What this means for you
- **In everyday life:** the next time your phone rings with a panicked voice or an official-sounding "agent", you'll hang up first and call back on a number you trust, before any money or information moves.
- **For your business or work:** anyone who handles invoices, supplier requests, or payments should confirm a new or urgent payment request by calling back on a number already on file, and a team can agree on a check word the way families do.
- **If you're just getting started:** do one thing today — text one family member the safe-word idea from Step 6, and save reportfraud.ftc.gov in your bookmarks.

## Try it now
Right now, open your messaging app and text one trusted person: *"If I ever call you in a panic and ask for money or codes, ask me for our safe word. The word is [pick something unusual, like 'platypus' or 'silver-spoon']."* That one text takes under two minutes and is the single most useful habit in this guide.
